description: Hi! We are Team Chipettes for the Delhi event, tackling "Dancing with the SARs." We're looking for passionate teammates to join us! We bring strengths in coding, web dev, writing, data analysis, and AI/ML. We'd love to connect with fellow innovators, developers, and designers excited about earth science data to build a creative, impactful solution together. Join us!
summary:
GOD’S EYE VIEW is an age-adaptive escape guide for people living in flood- and tsunami-prone areas. It uses satellite radar (SAR) to find flooded ground and guides each person along a dry route to the nearest bunker.

SAR sees through storm clouds and darkness, when optical satellites go blind. We turn SAR water masks and elevation data into a live safety map and re-plan the route as the water rises. The app adapts to who is using it:

Children (8-15): a friendly guide, simple steps and voice help.
Adults (16-59): ETAs, flood depth and alternative shelters.
Seniors (60+): large text, one step at a time and one-tap calls to family or emergency services.

A government dashboard maps responsive and non-responsive people in real time and flags priority search zones. This gives rescuers figures to work with.

Children, older adults and anyone cut off from reliable information are most at risk in floods and tsunamis. GOD’S EYE VIEW turns satellite data into clear, personal guidance when those at risk can no longer see the danger themselves.

(The prototype currently uses simulated data. The production design uses Sentinel-1 and NISAR.)
details:
GOD’S EYE VIEW by Team Chipettes

What it does and how it works
GOD’S EYE VIEW guides people in flood- and tsunami-prone areas to the nearest safe bunker along a dry route. Radar satellites (SAR) detect water through clouds and at night, because water reflects the radar away and appears dark. The app turns that flood mask and elevation data into a live map and finds the safest path with a routing algorithm (Dijkstra) that avoids flooded and low-lying ground. When the water level changes, the route is recalculated. After a person logs in with their age, the interface adapts to them.

  • Ages 8–15: a friendly guide, big arrows, a progress bar, read-aloud and a help button.
  • Ages 16–59: ETA, flood depth, alternative shelters, full directions and live location sharing.
  • Ages 60+: large text, one step at a time and one-tap calls to family or 112.

A separate government dashboard shows people as dots on the map. It counts those who are responsive, those with no signal for 60 minutes or more, and those already in bunkers, and flags priority search zones. A person with no signal for an hour is treated as presumed lost for planning, not confirmed.

Benefits

  • It works when optical satellites can’t see, in storms and at night.
  • Guidance fits the user’s age, so children, adults and older people each get what they can use in an emergency.
  • It re-plans automatically as water spreads, instead of giving a fixed evacuation map.
  • Rescuers get real-time counts and priority zones rather than guesses.

Intended impact
We want fewer people stranded or lost in water disasters, especially children and older adults. We also want faster, better-targeted rescue, and a way to turn open NASA and ESA radar data into guidance that ordinary families can act on.

Tools and technology

  • Prototype: HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, drawn on the HTML5 canvas, with the browser’s built-in voice (Web Speech API) for read-aloud. It runs in any browser, including phones, with no installation.
  • Map and routing: procedurally generated terrain with shading and contour lines, plus a flood mask computed from water level and elevation. A Dijkstra shortest-path algorithm with penalties for flooded ground does the routing.
    • Sentinel-1 and NISAR SAR data (for example via NASA’s ASF HyP3)
    • Open elevation data (SRTM or Copernicus DEM) and OpenStreetMap roads
    • The open-source gods-eye-view 3D globe for visualisation
    • GPS and mobile alerts
  • Hardware: none beyond ordinary laptops and phones. The prototype needs no special hardware.

What is creative about it

  • It uses SAR as a human-safety tool for children and seniors, not only as an expert analysis product.
  • One app produces three different interfaces from the same data, and a fourth for governments.
  • The “no signal for an hour” count gives rescuers a figure to plan with, and it is clearly labelled as presumed, not confirmed.
  • The slider lets anyone watch the flood grow and the route change.

Factors we considered

  • Age and accessibility: simple words for children, large text for seniors and voice guidance. Local languages are planned.
  • Safety: the app never sends anyone through water. If the only route is flooded, it tells them to stay on high ground and call for help. Official warnings come first.
  • Connectivity: networks fail in disasters, so the production version needs offline mode and low-bandwidth use.
  • Privacy: minimise stored location data, especially for children, and make sharing location opt-in.
  • Honesty about data: the prototype’s terrain, flood mask, people and bunkers are simulated, and we say so.
  • Accuracy and latency: SAR passes are not continuous, and flood masks must be validated before being used for real evacuation decisions.
  • Credit and licensing: the project builds on the open-source gods-eye-view repo and on NASA and ESA data, and these must be credited.
